A concise, linked glossary of platform-engineering concepts, research and reusable implementations. Start with a term, open its topic overview, then follow links to deeper analysis, primary sources or working code. Only published material is linked as a completed guide.

docs.title: How to read and contribute
docs.text:
Glossary → topic README → detailed guide → runnable implementation. Topic READMEs give a brief problem statement, conclusion and ranked recommendations. Detailed analysis belongs in linked details.md; actual tested code belongs in labs/, modules/ or tooling/. Avoid duplicating explanations and never publish private or employer-specific material.

For conventions, see documentation standards. For AI-assisted updates, see AGENTS.md and the GitHub workflow.

docs.title: Publishing as a website
docs.text: These relative Markdown links work in GitHub and can be used by a static documentation generator such as MkDocs Material. No site is deployed yet. Prefer GitHub Pages for this GitHub-hosted source; GitLab Pages is an alternative if a GitLab-hosted publishing workflow is desired.

docs.title: Agent instructions — Platform Engineering Monorepo
docs.text: This public repository is the source of truth for committed engineering projects, labs, Terraform modules, scripts, manifests, container images, architectures, troubleshooting and technical knowledge—not an archive of chat transcripts. main is the reference branch.

docs.title: Workflow triggers and skills
docs.text:
• Ordinary technical question: Answer normally; do not automatically inspect or change the repository.
  • Explicit request to search/review/compare repository knowledge: Follow repository-knowledge-review. Search code and documentation across the repo. Identify what is covered, related and improvable, or new. Read-only unless the user separately authorizes edits.
  • Explicit request to create/save/update/append/commit, including "Add this to my repository": Follow knowledge-curation. Inspect current implementations first; improve and reuse them when possible.
  • Never assume unrelated historical conversations exist in GitHub; only committed files and the current session are available.

docs.title: Structure and reuse
docs.text:
• labs/: integrated runnable scenarios (EKS, GitLab runners, identity, networking, GitOps, image builds). Start actual scenario folders when implementing their code; see labs/README.md.
  • modules/: independently reusable infrastructure components, currently organized under modules/terraform/.
  • tooling/: container images, CLI/devcontainer tooling, Bash/Python scripts and validation.
  • engineering-reference/: short educational examples, concepts, troubleshooting, architecture and authoritative source links. Navigate using INDEX.md and apply content standards.
  • .agents/skills/: task instructions. AGENTS.md: repository-wide policy.
  • Prefer one canonical implementation or explanation with cross-links instead of copying code or splitting one topic into duplicate files. When useful, tag guide pages by multiple technologies and link them to labs; keep navigation current.
  • Keep runnable examples reproducible and specify dependencies, usage, security tradeoffs and validation. Run relevant tests when possible; never claim tests succeeded unless actually run.
  • Content must be independently created using public and synthetic data. Never include work-proprietary code/architecture, secret values, private account identifiers, personal information or internal logs. The root .gitignore is helpful but not a secret scanner or a guarantee.

docs.title: GitHub publication
docs.text:
• Only after explicit request: Create a descriptive feature branch from main, make scoped edits, commit to it, verify the changed files and commit through GitHub, and create a PR targeting main.
  • Return the PR URL and full SHA. Never automatically merge into main; never force-push, delete repositories, or change branch protections without explicit consent.
  • Do not require the user to run Git commands or use Codespaces. If write access or validation fails, report the limitation truthfully.

docs.title: Reading the handbook
docs.text:
Open the overview PNG

This is a technical book with two reading modes:

  1. Read in order: Foundations → Infrastructure → CI/CD → GitOps → Security → Operations → Practice. Each part introduces the concepts needed by later chapters.
  2. Find an answer: use the glossary, topic index, or the website's built-in Search. A topic overview leads to ranked recommendations and then detailed analysis.

The book is intentionally honest about its maturity: only four research topics are published as chapters so far. Other parts are editorial introductions and roadmaps, not claims that the underlying guides or labs exist.

docs.title: Table of contents
docs.text:
Part Core questions Current reading I. Foundations What do containers, Kubernetes and networking provide? Conceptual roadmap II. AWS and Infrastructure How are EKS and infrastructure upgraded safely? EKS rollback III. Containers and CI/CD How should GitLab jobs build and publish images? Buildah / ECR IV. GitOps and Deployment How do Flux and Helm declare and reconcile desired state? GitOps context V. Security How do we contain privileged workloads? Runner isolation VI. Operations How do we discover unsupported dependencies? EOL inventory VII. Practice How do we turn guidance into tested implementations? Lab and tooling catalog

Editorial rule: chapter introductions explain why the topic matters; linked topic README.md files summarize the problem and recommendations; details.md provides depth and primary sources; implementation files live in labs/, modules/ and tooling/.

docs.title: Part I — Foundations
docs.text:
Open the overview PNG

Platform engineering builds repeatable environments by combining operating systems, containers, orchestration, identity and networks. A container packages a process and dependencies; Kubernetes schedules and reconciles containers, but does not by itself guarantee workload isolation or lifecycle support.

docs.title: Concepts to establish
docs.text:
Concept Why it matters Where it appears later Linux namespaces and capabilities Define process boundaries and privilege Runner isolation OCI images and registries Define build and distribution artifacts Buildah and ECR Kubernetes scheduling and networking Define placement and communication Runner isolation Declarative configuration Separates desired from observed state EOL scanning

Status: This is a reading roadmap, not a completed foundational tutorial. Continue to Part II — Infrastructure.

docs.title: Part II — AWS and Infrastructure
docs.text:
Open the overview PNG

Infrastructure as code describes resources, while the AWS APIs and Kubernetes ecosystem determine what operations are actually supported. EKS upgrades illustrate why a Terraform provider's capabilities, AWS rollback rules, node compatibility and add-on lifecycle must be evaluated independently.

← Foundations · Next: Containers and CI/CD →

docs.title: Part III — Containers and CI/CD
docs.text:
Open the overview PNG

A CI job is a workload with compute privileges, cloud identity and network access. Container builds must distinguish how an image is built, how the job authenticates to push it, and how Kubernetes authenticates to pull it.

docs.title: Published chapter
docs.text:
Buildah with GitLab Kubernetes executor and ECR — overview → detailed analysis.

See also privileged runner isolation.

docs.title: Further subjects
docs.text:
GitLab Runner Helm values, OIDC/IRSA, rootless Podman, registry mirrors and pipeline testing remain future chapter candidates.

← Infrastructure · Next: GitOps →

docs.title: Part IV — GitOps and Deployment
docs.text:
Open the overview PNG

Flux reconciles declared Kubernetes resources from Git and OCI sources. Helm charts simplify packaging but introduce a key distinction: chart versions are not necessarily application versions, and the rendered chart can introduce multiple workloads and images.

The currently published treatment is the Flux/Helm EOL inventory overview and its technical analysis.

Dedicated Flux source-controller, HelmRelease, Kustomize and reconciliation chapters remain planned, not published.

← CI/CD · Next: Security →

docs.title: Part V — Security
docs.text:
Open the overview PNG

Security controls operate at different boundaries: Kyverno governs admission, Calico/Cilium govern allowed network traffic, IRSA governs AWS permissions, and node isolation limits co-tenancy. None alone makes privileged DinD equivalent to an unprivileged workload.

docs.title: Published chapter
docs.text:
Privileged GitLab runners and DinD — overview → detailed analysis.

For software supply-chain lifecycle risks, continue to EOL inventory.

← GitOps · Next: Operations →

docs.title: Part VI — Operations and Lifecycle
docs.text:
Open the overview PNG

An EKS platform has multiple release clocks: Kubernetes, add-ons, controllers, Helm charts, deployed applications, images and node operating systems. Operational safety requires knowing both what Git declares and what the cluster actually runs.

docs.title: Published chapter
docs.text:
Flux, Helm, Terraform and EKS EOL inventory — overview → detailed analysis and validation.

Related reading: EKS upgrade and rollback.

← Security · Next: Practice →

docs.title: EKS rollback and Terraform
docs.text:
← Glossary · Topic index

Open the overview PNG

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: An EKS version upgrade may introduce incompatibilities; AWS rollback availability does not imply Terraform provider support.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Verify AWS rollback eligibility and the pinned Terraform provider's capabilities, and maintain a tested workload and add-on recovery plan.

docs.title: Ranked recommendations
docs.text: Priority Recommendation Impact P0 Confirm AWS rollback prerequisites and constraints Avoid unsupported recovery assumptions P1 Check the pinned Terraform provider schema Distinguish API and provider capabilities P1 Test workload, node and add-on recovery Control-plane rollback is not complete recovery P2 Reconcile Terraform after any out-of-band action Prevent drift

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Detailed analysis, validation and references · Related topic index

Research summary; implementation and runtime validation are not implied.

docs.title: Detailed analysis
docs.text: ← Topic overview · Glossary

docs.title: EKS rollback and Terraform — detailed analysis
Problem
docs.text: An EKS control-plane upgrade can create compatibility or workload issues. Operators need to know whether a rollback feature can be used through Terraform.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: AWS API capabilities and Terraform AWS provider resource support are distinct. An AWS announcement does not prove that aws_eks_cluster exposes a matching rollback argument or operation. Rollback eligibility, supported version transitions, time windows and effects on nodes/add-ons must be checked against current AWS and provider documentation.

docs.title: Ranked recommendations
docs.text: Rank Impact Recommendation Rationale 1 Critical Validate the currently supported AWS rollback API, prerequisites and constraints before upgrading Avoids assuming recoverability 2 High Inspect the pinned Terraform AWS provider schema and changelog for rollback support Distinguishes provider support from AWS feature availability 3 High Maintain a tested recovery plan for nodes, add-ons, workloads and CRDs Control-plane rollback alone may not restore compatibility 4 Medium Use staging upgrades and compatibility checks before production Reduces upgrade failures 5 Medium Document out-of-band recovery operations and reconcile Terraform state afterward Avoids configuration drift

docs.text:

  • Terraform AWS provider EKS cluster

docs.title: Buildah and ECR on GitLab Kubernetes executor
docs.text:
← Glossary · Topic index

Open the overview PNG

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: CI image builds require ECR authentication without static AWS credentials or unnecessary privileged DinD.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Use least-privilege IRSA and verify Buildah rootless behavior, image-pull authentication and ECR push authentication separately.

docs.title: Ranked recommendations
docs.text: Priority Recommendation Impact P0 Use dedicated least-privilege IRSA service accounts Avoid static credentials P1 Validate rootless Buildah on the target cluster Reduce host exposure P1 Test AWS CLI ECR login or verified credential-helper support Ensure working short-lived auth P2 Pin build image versions and enforce scoped egress Improve repeatability

docs.text:
Detailed analysis, validation and references · Related topic index

Research summary; implementation and runtime validation are not implied.

docs.title: Detailed analysis
docs.text: ← Topic overview · Glossary

docs.title: Buildah and ECR on GitLab Kubernetes executor — detailed analysis
Problem
docs.text: Container builds in GitLab's Kubernetes executor need AWS ECR authentication without embedding long-lived registry credentials or unnecessarily enabling privileged Docker-in-Docker.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Buildah can build OCI images without a Docker daemon, but rootless operation depends on the container image, user namespaces, storage driver and cluster security settings. IRSA supplies AWS credentials to the job service account, not automatically to every arbitrary image-pull mechanism. The ECR credential helper and aws ecr get-login-password are different authentication approaches; validate the helper's compatibility with the chosen tool.

docs.title: Ranked recommendations
docs.text: Rank Impact Recommendation Rationale 1 Critical Use a dedicated least-privilege Kubernetes service account with IRSA for build jobs Avoids static AWS keys 2 High Prefer unprivileged Buildah after validating user namespaces and storage behavior Reduces host exposure 3 High Use ECR login via AWS CLI and short-lived token, or verify credential-helper integration end to end Avoids assuming helper support 4 High Separate Kubernetes image-pull authentication from in-job image push authentication Different components resolve credentials 5 Medium Pin Buildah/AWS CLI image versions and test push/pull with the actual executor Improves reproducibility 6 Medium Apply scoped network policies and registry endpoint access Reduces unnecessary egress

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Confirm the job's AWS identity, successful ECR login, image build/push, non-root permissions and denial of unrelated AWS actions. Document any environment-specific user-namespace prerequisites.

docs.text:

docs.text:
← Glossary · Topic index

Open the overview PNG

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A Flux repository may deploy unsupported applications and add-ons even when Helm charts are pinned.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Resolve chart, app, image and add-on versions independently. Scan desired state and optionally compare with running EKS workloads; treat unmapped dependencies as visible coverage gaps.

docs.title: Ranked recommendations
docs.text: Priority Recommendation Impact P0 Inventory rendered images and resolve app versions Prevent false lifecycle conclusions P0 Check installed EKS add-ons against AWS compatibility data Identify incompatibilities P1 Support Flux references, Terraform parsing and distinct unknown statuses Improve coverage and accuracy P1 Preserve GitLab CI failures and publish auditable reports Make findings actionable P2 Schedule scans and automate proposed upgrades Reduce remediation delay

Research summary; implementation and runtime validation are not implied.

docs.title: Detailed analysis
docs.text: ← Topic overview · Glossary

docs.title: EOL scanning across Flux, Helm, Terraform and EKS — detailed analysis
Problem
docs.text: A GitOps repository can pin apparently current Helm charts while deploying unsupported applications, images, controllers, Kubernetes APIs or EKS add-ons. A useful scanner must identify unsupported dependencies and disclose gaps in coverage without misclassifying chart releases as application releases.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
Our platform-engineering discussions span EKS managed node groups and Karpenter, Terraform, GitLab Kubernetes runners, Flux, Helm, Kyverno, Calico/Cilium, ECR, CSI and secrets drivers. Scan these as separate lifecycle surfaces:

  • Git desired state: Flux HelmRelease (both spec.chart.spec and spec.chartRef), HelmRepository, OCIRepository, Kustomization, ordinary Kubernetes YAML, Terraform EKS/add-on/module declarations, and container build definitions.
  • Resolved releases: Helm chart version is not reliably the workload app version. Obtain chart metadata (appVersion), render manifests and collect all images (including init containers and sidecars); track images by digest when possible. For umbrella charts, scan every component independently.
  • Actual cluster: Git alone cannot prove which images and versions are running. Optionally reconcile against live workloads, Flux status, installed Helm releases, EKS control-plane version, managed add-ons and node AMIs.
  • Support sources: Use endoflife.date where a verified product/cycle mapping exists, then official upstream support/release policies, AWS EKS add-on compatibility APIs and vendor release notes. An image vulnerability scan is complementary, not proof of lifecycle support.

Do not assume every named component has a current endoflife.date product slug or that its cycle is its full semantic version. Validate mappings and API response schema before enforcement. aws eks describe-addon-versions reports compatible versions, not the currently installed add-on or its end-of-support date; use describe-addon for installed version and vendor documentation for support.

docs.title: Ranked recommendations
docs.text: Rank Impact Recommendation Why P0 Critical Separate chart, application, image, Kubernetes API, EKS add-on and node/AMI lifecycle records Prevents false EOL assessments P0 Critical Render Flux-managed Helm charts and inspect all resulting containers, including sidecars/init containers Finds dependencies invisible in chart metadata P0 Critical Inventory installed EKS add-ons and compare with describe-addon-versions for the target Kubernetes version Detects compatibility issues without inventing EOL dates P1 High Resolve HelmRelease chart references, OCI tags/digests, Kustomize overlays and Terraform variables/modules Avoids missed or incorrectly parsed versions P1 High Keep UNMAPPED, UNKNOWN, UNPINNED, UNSUPPORTED, WARN and OK distinct Makes missing evidence visible P1 High Fail CI only on validated unsupported/EOL findings; report uncertain cases and enforce a separate coverage threshold Reduces false-positive pipeline failures P1 High Preserve scanner exit status, pin dependencies and publish JSON/SARIF plus human-readable artifacts Makes GitLab findings actionable and auditable P2 Medium Add weekly scheduled scans and Renovate-driven version-update MRs Shortens remediation lead time P2 Medium Compare Git desired state with live EKS/Flux resources using read-only credentials Finds drift and unmanaged workloads P2 Medium Assign owners to unmapped components and periodically verify authoritative lifecycle links Expands coverage systematically

docs.title: Suggested implementation
docs.text:
Keep this as a reusable tooling project, not a single large Bash/Python snippet embedded in this guide. A future implementation could use:

tooling/eol-scanner/
  README.md
  eol-map.yaml
  requirements.txt
  scripts/eol_scan.py
  tests/
  examples/gitlab-ci.yml

Mapping records should specify component type, source of the resolved version, product/cycle normalization, official fallback source and optional exception expiry. Avoid mapping kube-prometheus-stack directly to the Prometheus lifecycle: it can deploy Prometheus, Alertmanager, exporters, Grafana and more.

A safe scanner pipeline has stages for discovery, resolution, lookup, evaluation and reporting. Cache rate-limited upstream API responses; handle network errors explicitly. Compare dates only after parsing a valid lifecycle policy. Do not interpret eol: false as indefinite support; it means no known EOL date in that source.

docs.title: GitLab CI reliability
docs.text: Use a pinned scanner image with locked dependencies and a tested entrypoint. If streaming output through tee, enable set -o pipefail in a shell that supports it, or write the report directly and propagate the scanner's status. Publish artifacts with when: always and set failure policy intentionally for merge requests versus scheduled audits.

docs.title: AWS checks
docs.text:
• aws eks describe-cluster: running Kubernetes version.
  • aws eks list-addons and aws eks describe-addon: installed managed add-ons and versions.
  • aws eks describe-addon-versions --kubernetes-version ... --addon-name ...: available compatible versions, not EOL proof.
  • Track AWS VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI and EFS CSI where applicable; distinguish AWS-managed add-ons from self-managed Helm installations.
  • Inventory Secrets Store CSI Driver and AWS Secrets Manager provider separately, since a provider's lifecycle need not match the driver's.
  • For managed node groups and Karpenter, inspect AMI/OS release lifecycle independently of the control-plane version.

docs.title: Validation and acceptance criteria
docs.text:
1. Fixture coverage: HelmRelease direct chart and chartRef, OCIRepository tag/digest, Kustomize overlay, Terraform variable-based cluster version, and multiple YAML documents.
  2. Chart fixture with differing chart/app versions and images for init containers and sidecars.
  3. API fixtures for EOL date, true, false, unknown cycle, missing slug, timeout and malformed data.
  4. EKS add-on fixture that distinguishes installed version, compatible versions and missing support dates.
  5. GitLab test proves a real FAIL returns nonzero even when output is piped to tee.
  6. Report preserves source URL, check date, version provenance, uncertainty and remediation owner.
  7. Scanner does not require production cluster access for static checks; optional runtime reconciliation uses least-privilege read-only credentials.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This is an engineering design/review tailored from the supplied Claude discussion and our platform engineering topics. It is not a tested implementation against a real Flux repository. The sample script's broad YAML parsing, regex Terraform parsing, chart-to-app mapping, guessed lifecycle cycles and unguarded network lookups should not be adopted without the corrections above.

docs.title: Privileged GitLab runners and DinD
docs.text:
← Glossary · Topic index

Open the overview PNG

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Privileged Docker-in-Docker jobs can compromise node isolation; Kubernetes namespaces alone do not remove host-level risk.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Prefer verified unprivileged builds. If privileged jobs remain necessary, isolate them on dedicated disposable nodes with narrowly scoped admission, network and IAM controls.

docs.title: Ranked recommendations
docs.text: Priority Recommendation Impact P0 Prefer rootless Buildah/BuildKit where supported Reduce privileged execution P0 Use dedicated tainted and short-lived nodes Limit co-tenancy and persistence P1 Enforce Kyverno exception scoping and Calico/Cilium network policy Reduce lateral movement P1 Limit IRSA and registry access Reduce cloud and network blast radius

docs.text:
Detailed analysis, validation and references · Related topic index

Research summary; implementation and runtime validation are not implied.

docs.title: Detailed analysis
docs.text: ← Topic overview · Glossary

docs.title: Privileged GitLab runners and DinD — detailed analysis
Problem
docs.text: Docker-in-Docker builds on Kubernetes may require privileged containers. A compromised build can gain capabilities unavailable to ordinary pods; namespace separation alone does not provide node isolation.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Privileged pods can expose the host kernel and node resources. IRSA restricts AWS API permissions, not Linux privileges. Kyverno can control admission, Calico can enforce pod network policy, and Karpenter can provision dedicated nodes, but none alone makes privileged workloads equivalent to unprivileged ones. Image pulls, CI job downloads and arbitrary build-time curl requests have different egress requirements.

docs.title: Ranked recommendations
docs.text: Rank Impact Recommendation Rationale 1 Critical Prefer rootless BuildKit/Buildah or another verified unprivileged build path Removes privileged DinD requirement where feasible 2 Critical Run privileged builds on dedicated, tainted, disposable nodes and restrict scheduling Reduces co-tenancy and persistence after compromise; not a host-escape guarantee 3 High Deny privileged pods by default with a narrowly scoped Kyverno exception Prevents unrelated workloads from inheriting the exception 4 High Apply Calico default-deny ingress/egress and explicitly allow DNS, approved registries and required services Reduces lateral movement and uncontrolled network reachability 5 High Scope IRSA permissions to minimum ECR actions and resources; prevent access to node credentials Limits cloud-side blast radius 6 Medium Separate registry traffic through approved mirrors/proxies and govern arbitrary build egress independently Keeps required downloads possible without claiming a total internet block 7 Medium Rotate nodes, scan images, audit exceptions and validate isolation with adversarial tests Detects drift and limits exposure duration

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Test a denied privileged pod outside the exception, cross-job connectivity, access to metadata/credentials, registry pull/push, proxy bypass, node placement and teardown. Do not claim parity with unprivileged pods.

docs.title: Documentation standards
docs.text:
Use progressive disclosure: root glossary → topic index → topic README → details.md → implementation.

Level File Content 1 Root README.md Alphabetical, one-line glossary with links; no lengthy explanations 2 Topic README.md Problem, concise answer, 3–5 impact-ranked recommendations, next links 3 Topic details.md Deeper analysis, tradeoffs, validation and authoritative sources 4 labs/, modules/, tooling/ Runnable code, usage, dependencies and verified tests

For a new topic, search the entire repository first. Enhance the canonical guide instead of creating duplicates. Use relative Markdown links, descriptive link text and cross-links between related subjects. Never link to nonexistent implementations as if they were completed.

Keep recommendations in a compact table with priority (P0 critical, P1 high, P2 medium), action and reason. Distinguish verified, proposed, and unknown claims. Cite primary documentation and note time/version sensitivity. Avoid irrelevant conversation drift, private infrastructure, secrets and employer material.

Place detailed code examples in reusable implementation folders rather than inflating overviews. Update the root glossary and topic index whenever a new canonical topic is published.

docs.title: Optional website
docs.text: Markdown must remain readable in GitHub and compatible with MkDocs. A future MkDocs Material site can provide full-text search, navigation and glossary browsing; deploy via GitHub Pages or GitLab Pages only after the publishing workflow is explicitly selected. Do not assume a site is live.

docs.title: Ebook illustration policy
docs.text:
Use a topic-specific PNG where a visual clarifies architecture, data flow, trust boundaries, state transitions or operational decision-making. Place diagram.png next to the chapter or topic README that embeds it, with descriptive alt text. Link to a deeper technical guide rather than treating the picture as the implementation. Prefer one meaningful diagram to decorative screenshots or duplicated generic illustrations. Do not add images to empty placeholders or directories that have no substantive content.

Review every diagram against the associated analysis: distinguish desired from actual state, permissions from isolation, and compatibility from EOL. Keep labels legible at ebook width, preserve the explanatory text for search/accessibility, and verify that every image link resolves. If a visual repeats an existing guide diagram in a chapter introduction, keep the copies synchronized when the underlying explanation changes.

docs.title: Diagram production standard
docs.text: The authoritative editable source is a local diagram.mmd beside the README; diagram.png is a generated artifact, not hand-drawn decoration. Use professional architecture conventions: named system boundaries, explicit flow direction, distinguish control plane from data plane, meaningful edge labels, consistent neutral palette, readable type and accurate trust boundaries. Diagrams must match the text and be specific to their folder. Do not copy one generic PNG into multiple unrelated topics. The GitHub Actions diagram renderer uses Mermaid configuration to regenerate all PNGs when source diagrams change. A diagram must not be treated as validated until the renderer succeeds.

docs.title: Using ChatGPT to commit directly to GitHub
docs.text: This repository was used to verify that ChatGPT can create a GitHub branch, commit a file, and read it back through a connected GitHub integration without opening a Codespace, running Git commands locally, or copying code into a terminal.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Sign in to ChatGPT.
  2. Open ChatGPT's Settings → Plugins (or the Plugins area in the chat sidebar) and connect the GitHub integration. Complete the GitHub authorization flow and grant access to the repository you want to edit. Available screens and permissions can vary by account.
  3. Confirm the repository is available to the integration. This test used platform-engineering-labz/platform-engineering.
  4. Use a branch instead of writing directly to main when testing.

Security: Only authorize the repositories and permissions needed. A GitHub connection does not imply that ChatGPT has access to every repository or that every write is allowed. Repository permissions, organization policies, and branch protections still apply.

docs.title: Step 1 — Find the connected repository
docs.text:
Ask ChatGPT:

Find my connected GitHub repository platform-engineering-labz/platform-engineering.

ChatGPT used its connected GitHub repository search to find the repository and confirm its default branch was main.

docs.title: Step 2 — Create a test branch
docs.text:
Ask ChatGPT:

Create branch test/chatgpt-commit from main in
platform-engineering-labz/platform-engineering.
Do not modify main.

ChatGPT invoked the GitHub integration's branch-creation operation with:

  • Repository: platform-engineering-labz/platform-engineering
  • Base reference: main
  • New branch: test/chatgpt-commit

View the test branch.

docs.title: Step 3 — Commit a new file
docs.text:
Ask ChatGPT:

On branch test/chatgpt-commit, create chatgpt-commit-test.txt
with a short timestamped GitHub connection test message.
Commit it with the message:
test: verify ChatGPT GitHub commit access

ChatGPT used the GitHub integration's file-creation operation, specifying the repository, file path, UTF-8 content, commit message, and explicit target branch. The integration wrote the file and returned this commit SHA:

2daff3c6c24ba53ddc3c4a4f86d5f1af3c1372d7
  • View the verified test commit
  • View the committed test file

The test file contains a timestamp labeled approximately 2026-10-19 00:21 America/Chicago. That timestamp was supplied in the test content; it is not an independently verified GitHub commit timestamp.

docs.title: Step 4 — Verify the commit
docs.text:
Ask ChatGPT:

Read chatgpt-commit-test.txt from test/chatgpt-commit,
compare test/chatgpt-commit with main, and report the
commit SHA and changes. Confirm main was not modified.

ChatGPT performed two independent checks using the GitHub integration:

  1. Fetch file: Read chatgpt-commit-test.txt from test/chatgpt-commit and confirmed the expected content was present.
  2. Compare commits: Compared main with test/chatgpt-commit. GitHub reported the test branch 1 commit ahead, 0 behind, with one new file and three added lines.

At verification time, main remained at commit 6846354419f887c69707a16c1e3f232681b4c0ee. This confirmed the test commit was on the feature branch, not main.

Compare the test branch against main

docs.title: Step 5 — Repeat the workflow
docs.text:
You can use a single prompt for the complete process:

In my connected GitHub repository OWNER/REPO:
1. Create branch test/chatgpt-commit from main.
2. Create chatgpt-commit-test.txt containing a short timestamped test message.
3. Commit the file to the test branch, not main.
4. Read the file back from the test branch.
5. Compare the test branch against main.
6. Give me the GitHub commit URL, full commit SHA, and verification results.
Do not modify main.

Replace OWNER/REPO, branch, and filename as appropriate. If the branch or file already exists, use a new test name or ask ChatGPT to inspect the existing file before updating it. A create-file operation cannot overwrite an existing file; an update needs its current blob SHA.

docs.title: Quick workflow — "Add this to my repository"
docs.text:
Once the GitHub integration is connected and the standing instructions below are saved, you can ask ChatGPT to prepare a pull request with a short message:

Add this to my repository

Send that message with the code, explanation, or requested change you want added, or use it as a follow-up to material already discussed in the conversation. For example:

Create a Terraform example for an AWS EKS cluster.
Add this to my repository.

To make this shorthand work reliably across new conversations, save the following under ChatGPT settings → Personalization → Custom Instructions:

When I say "Add this to my repository," use my connected GitHub integration
and the repository platform-engineering-labz/platform-engineering.

Automatically:
1. Create a descriptive feature branch from main.
2. Create or update the requested files.
3. Commit the changes to the feature branch.
4. Create a pull request targeting main.
5. Verify that the changes were successfully committed.
6. Provide a direct link to the pull request so I can review and merge it myself.

Never automatically merge into main.
Do not ask for confirmation for routine file changes I explicitly request.
Do not require me to run Git commands or use Codespaces.
Never force-push, delete repositories, or change branch protections
without explicit authorization.

What happens next: ChatGPT creates a branch, commits the files, opens a pull request, and returns a link. You review the changes in the repository's pull requests and choose Merge pull request yourself. The prompt does not authorize ChatGPT to merge into main.

The GitHub integration must remain connected and have sufficient repository permissions. Custom Instructions guide ChatGPT's workflow but do not bypass GitHub authorization, reviews, or branch protection rules.

docs.title: Updating an existing README
docs.text: For an existing file, ChatGPT first reads the file from the intended branch to obtain its contents and current blob SHA, then submits the complete replacement contents and that blob SHA through the GitHub integration's update-file operation. This protects against blindly overwriting a file that has changed.

Note: This guide records what worked in this specific connected ChatGPT session. GitHub integration availability, connection setup, and authorized write operations can differ by account and repository.

docs.text:

This area is for runnable, multi-component demonstrations, not stand-alone notes. Each lab should contain its own README, prerequisites, architecture, reproducible manifests/code, a test/validation path, teardown instructions, and security considerations. Use synthetic identifiers; never reuse work systems or configurations.

docs.title: Reusable modules
docs.text:
Open the overview PNG

Use this directory for reusable, tested components shared by multiple labs. A module should have clear inputs/outputs or interfaces, a README with usage examples, version constraints where applicable, and a verification method.

  • Terraform modules — reusable infrastructure modules; no published modules yet.

Prefer a small independent module over copying configuration into multiple labs. Do not publish account-specific or employer-derived settings.

docs.text:
